newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF tells DKB to halt new loans as part of penalty.
newsitem.headline: MOF tells DKB to halt new loans as part of penalty.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday it had ordered Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd to suspend new loan business from August 6 until December 31 as part of penalties for its illegal loans to a "sokaiya" racketeer.
New corporate loans will be prohibited completely as well as those for individuals, except for housing loans, it said.
MOF also said it had suspended DKB from participating in auctions and underwriting public bonds, including Japanese government bonds (JBGs), municipal bonds and government-guaranteed bonds.
The ministry also barred the bank from opening new branches or offices either domestically or overseas from August 6 until August 5, 1998.

It also said it would prohibit DKB from conducting sales of investment trusts at its branches, making use of holding companies, or liquidating assets by new methods. Such steps are due to be liberalised as part of Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
The ministry also ordered DKB to draw up steps to improve its in-house operations and submit details of such steps to the ministry by September 19.

MOF said the details of the steps must be concrete and the bank must specify dates of implementation. The ministry said it would ask DKB to make a report every six months on how the steps were being implemented.

The ministry said that as part of steps to improve DKB's operations, the bank should cut off ties with anti-social elements, such as sokaiya racketeers. It also said the bank should introduce a third party which would follow up to check whether the bank was actually carrying out measures to strengthen its internal supervision.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in a statement that the ministry strongly expects DKB and Nomura Securities Co Ltd, against which it also imposed penalties, to work towards regaining confidence.

Mitsuzuka's statement said: "In order to prevent a recurrence of such scandals, financial institutions must be conscious of their social responsibilities...revise their old management styles and regain the confidence of depositors and investors."

He also said in the statement that the ministry would take strict steps should further such violations occur and that it would work to strengthen its inspection and supervision as part of reform of the financial system.
